stem: Which of the following is a feature of monopolistic competition?

options.content: Many firms selling differentiated products
A single firm protected by barriers to entry
A few firms that depend on one another's decisions
Identical products sold by very many firms

explanation: Monopolistic competition has many firms selling differentiated products with easy entry and exit.

stem: Product differentiation means that

options.content: buyers see each firm's product as different from rivals' products
all firms sell the same product at the same price
firms differ only in the size of their output and workforce
the government sets the quality of the product
options.rationale: Differentiation is a firm's own choice.

explanation: Differentiation makes a firm's product different, in real or perceived ways, from those of rivals, so buyers do not see them as perfect substitutes.

stem: Which of the following is an example of non-price competition?

options.content: A salon cuts its price by half to attract more customers
A salon offers free braiding lessons and a loyalty card
A salon raises its price to cover costs
options.rationale: This is a price change, not non-price competition.

options.content: A salon closes for the day because of low sales
options.rationale: This is not a competitive strategy.

explanation: Advertising, branding and service quality compete for customers without cutting the price.

stem: In the short run a firm in monopolistic competition

options.content: always earns normal profit
options.rationale: Normal profit is the long-run result.

options.content: is a price-taker
options.rationale: It has some control over price because its product is differentiated.

options.content: cannot make a loss
options.rationale: It can make a loss if demand is weak.

options.content: can earn supernormal profit

explanation: It faces a downward-sloping demand curve and can earn supernormal profit or a loss, depending on demand and costs.

stem: In long-run equilibrium a monopolistically competitive firm

options.content: earns supernormal profit, because its product is unique
earns normal profit, with price equal to average total cost
produces at the lowest point of average cost
options.rationale: The tangency is on the falling part of ATC.

options.content: has a price equal to marginal cost

explanation: Entry removes supernormal profit, so the demand curve is tangent to ATC at the output where MC = MR: price equals ATC and profit is normal.

stem: New salons enter a market where existing salons earn supernormal profit. For an existing salon, the demand curve will

options.content: shift to the right and become much less price elastic
options.rationale: This would happen if demand for the product rose.

options.content: become perfectly inelastic
options.rationale: More substitutes make demand more elastic.

options.content: shift to the left and become more elastic
stay unchanged because entry has no effect

explanation: New firms offer close substitutes and take customers away, so each existing firm's demand falls (shifts left) and becomes more elastic.
hints: What does entry do to each existing firm's customers?

stem: Excess capacity in monopolistic competition means that

options.content: firms produce more than they can sell at the going price
options.rationale: The firm sells what it produces.

options.content: firms earn supernormal profit in the long run because of unused capacity
options.rationale: Profit is normal in the long run.

options.content: firms produce less than the output at which average cost is lowest
firms employ too many workers for their output
options.rationale: The concept concerns unused productive capacity.

explanation: In long-run equilibrium the firm produces on the falling part of ATC, below the output at which average cost is lowest.
hints: Compare the output chosen with the output at which ATC is lowest.

stem: A firm in monopolistic competition spends heavily on advertising. Compared with no advertising, the most likely immediate effect is a

options.content: fall in average total cost and a leftward shift of demand
options.rationale: Advertising costs money and aims to raise demand.

options.content: rise in marginal cost to the level of price
options.rationale: Advertising is mostly a fixed cost and does not set MC equal to price.

options.content: fall in the number of firms in the industry
options.rationale: Advertising does not by itself change entry.

options.content: rise in average total cost and, if successful, a rightward shift of demand

explanation: Advertising is a fixed cost that raises ATC; if it shifts demand to the right and makes it less elastic, the firm may sell more or charge more.
hints: Think about costs as well as demand.

stem: A fictional salon faces the demand curve P = 38 − 2Q (price in US\$, Q = customers a day), so MR = 38 − 4Q. Its marginal cost is a constant US\$10. Calculate its profit-maximising output.
explanation: 38 − 4Q = 10, so Q = 7 customers a day.

stem: The salon above produces 7 customers a day. Calculate the price it charges, in US\$.
explanation: P = 38 − 2 × 7 = US\$24 (not MC = 10, and not MR = 10).
workedSolution: 1. P = 38 − 2 × 7 = US\$24 (not MC = 10, and not MR = 10).
hints: Read the price from the demand curve.

stem: The salon sells 7 customers a day at US\$24. Its marginal cost is US\$10 and its total fixed cost is US\$72 a day. Calculate its profit, in US\$.
explanation:
1. TR = 24 × 7 = 168.
2. TC = 72 + 10 × 7 = 142.
3. Profit = 168 − 142 = US\$26 a day, which is supernormal.
workedSolution:
1. 1. TR = 24 × 7 = 168.
2. TC = 72 + 10 × 7 = 142.
3. Profit = 168 − 142 = US\$26 a day, which is supernormal.
hints: Total fixed cost is US\$72 a day.

stem: Entry shifts the salon's demand curve to P = 34 − 2Q (MR = 34 − 4Q). Marginal cost is US\$10 and total fixed cost is US\$72. Calculate the price in the new equilibrium, in US\$ (the firm now earns normal profit).
explanation: 34 − 4Q = 10 gives Q = 6; P = 34 − 12 = US\$22. Check: ATC = (72 + 60) ÷ 6 = US\$22, so profit is zero.
workedSolution: 1. 34 − 4Q = 10 gives Q = 6; P = 34 − 12 = US\$22. Check: ATC = (72 + 60) ÷ 6 = US\$22, so profit is zero.
hints: After entry the demand curve is P = 34 − 2Q.

stem: In long-run equilibrium a monopolistically competitive firm charges a price equal to its marginal cost.
explanation: False. Price equals average total cost (normal profit) and is above marginal cost, so there is allocative inefficiency.

stem: Match each market structure with the statement that fits its long-run position.

right.content: Supernormal profit can persist because entry is blocked
Price is set by the government
Price equals minimum ATC and marginal cost
Price equals ATC, above marginal cost; excess capacity

explanation: Entry removes supernormal profit in the first two structures; in monopoly, barriers prevent it.

stem: Complete the statement.

explanation: New firms take customers away, so demand shifts left.

stem: Name the long-run position of a monopolistically competitive firm in which the demand curve just touches the average total cost curve.
explanation: The tangency solution: price equals ATC at the output where MC = MR.

stem: State **three** features of monopolistic competition.

points.description: Many firms.
Differentiated products.
Easy entry and exit (no significant barriers).

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: There are many firms, each sells a differentiated product, and there is easy entry into and exit from the market.

explanation: Three features.

stem: Explain why firms in monopolistic competition earn only normal profit in the long run.

points.description: Supernormal profit attracts new firms because entry is easy.
New firms offer close substitutes, taking customers from existing firms.
Each firm's demand curve shifts left and becomes more elastic.
Entry continues until price equals ATC and supernormal profit disappears.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Supernormal profit attracts new firms because there are no barriers to entry. The new firms offer similar products and take customers from existing firms, so each firm's demand curve shifts to the left and becomes more elastic. This continues until the demand curve touches the average total cost curve, so that price equals average cost and only normal profit is earned.

explanation: Entry competes away profit.

stem: Assess the efficiency of monopolistic competition in the long run.

points.description: Not allocatively efficient: price is above marginal cost.
Not productively efficient: excess capacity, with output below the lowest-cost level.
Consumers gain variety and choice.
Judgement: some inefficiency, but variety may justify it.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: In the long run price is above marginal cost, so the market is not allocatively efficient, and firms operate with excess capacity, so it is not productively efficient. But consumers gain from a variety of differentiated products and from services tailored to their tastes, and the loss of efficiency is small compared with that of monopoly. On balance the inefficiency is modest and may be worth the choice it brings.

explanation: Weigh the inefficiency against variety.
hints: Allocative efficiency, productive efficiency and variety.

stem: A fictional restaurant in Mutare faces the demand curve P = 46 − 2Q (price in US\$, Q = meals in tens per day), so MR = 46 − 4Q. Its marginal cost is a constant US\$14 and its total fixed cost is US\$72 a day (illustrative data).

parts.label: (b)

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate the restaurant's profit, in US\$.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: What is likely to happen in the long run?

options.content: Existing restaurants leave and demand shifts right
options.rationale: Exit follows losses, not supernormal profit.

options.content: The restaurant becomes a price-taker
options.rationale: Differentiation keeps some control over price.

options.content: Profit rises further as costs fall
New restaurants enter and demand for this restaurant shifts left

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: State **two** ways in which the restaurant might compete without cutting its price.

points.description: A valid non-price method (quality, menu variety, location, service, advertising).
A second valid method.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: It could advertise and build a brand, and improve the quality and variety of its food and the speed of service.

explanation: Output 8, price US\$30, profit US\$56; entry will shift demand left and reduce profit.

stem: After entry the restaurant's demand curve is P = 38 − 2Q (MR = 38 − 4Q). Marginal cost is US\$14 and fixed cost is US\$72. The owner then spends an extra US\$24 a day on advertising, so total fixed cost is US\$96, and demand shifts to P = 42 − 2Q (MR = 42 − 4Q).

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the profit-maximising output before the advertising.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate profit before the advertising, in US\$.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate the profit-maximising output after the advertising.

parts.label: (d)

parts.stem: Explain how advertising can change a firm's position in monopolistic competition.

points.description: It aims to shift the demand curve to the right (more customers).
It may make demand less elastic by building brand loyalty.
It adds to fixed cost, so it raises average total cost.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Advertising aims to attract more customers, shifting demand to the right, and to build brand loyalty, which makes demand less elastic. But it is an extra fixed cost, so average total cost rises, and the benefit depends on the extra revenue exceeding that cost.

parts.label: (f)

points.description: Rivals can copy the strategy or advertise too.
New firms may enter, shifting demand back to the left.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Rival restaurants can advertise too, and any supernormal profit would attract new entrants, so demand would shift back to the left.

explanation: Advertising raises output from 6 to 7 and profit from 0 to US\$2, but at a higher fixed cost and only until rivals respond.
hints: MR = a − 4Q for demand P = a − 2Q.

stem: Assess whether monopolistic competition is a good market structure for consumers.

points.description: Consumers benefit from variety and choice.
Competition between many firms and easy entry keep profits at normal in the long run.
Firms compete on quality and service, not only price.
Price is above marginal cost: allocative inefficiency.
Excess capacity means productive inefficiency.
Advertising raises costs and prices, though it may inform consumers.
The loss is small compared with monopoly.
A justified judgement.

levels.descriptor: Two-sided, applied and developed, with a justified conclusion.
Some development of one side, limited application or conclusion.

answerSpec.modelAnswer: Monopolistic competition gives consumers a wide variety of products and services, and easy entry keeps profit at the normal level in the long run, so it is not exploitative. Firms compete on quality and service as well as on price. But price is above marginal cost, so it is not allocatively efficient, and firms operate with excess capacity, so it is not productively efficient. Advertising adds to cost, although it may also inform consumers. The loss of efficiency is small compared with monopoly. Overall, the market is good for consumers when they value variety and entry is free, although the prices are somewhat higher than in perfect competition.

explanation: Variety and free entry against excess capacity and higher price.
hints: Compare with perfect competition and monopoly.
